items.prose: An incident report from an invented recruitment firm. A recruiter pasted 40 candidates' CVs, with names, phone numbers and current salaries, into a public chatbot, and asked it to rank them for a trader role. It put candidates from two universities at the top, the two most past hires had come from. The recruiter sent the ranking to the client unchanged.

parts.question: Select all that apply: what was pasted that should not have been?

options.text: Candidates' names
Candidates' phone numbers
Candidates' current salaries
The words "trader role"
options.why: The job title is not personal data.

options.text: The request to rank them
options.why: A request is not data about anyone.

feedback.correct: Names, phone numbers and salaries: personal data about each candidate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for what identifies or describes a person.

explain.text: Names and phone numbers identify each candidate, and salaries are private details about them. None of it should go into a public tool without an approved tool and policy.

parts.question: What bias did the ranking show?

options.text: It favoured the universities past hires came from: bias from data
None at all: a chatbot has no opinions of its own
options.why: No opinions are needed. It ranked by the pattern of past hires.

options.text: Random noise, nothing systematic
options.why: Two universities at the top, matching past hires, is a pattern, not noise.

options.text: It found the best candidates
options.why: It found candidates who looked like past hires, which is not the same.

feedback.correct: It repeated the pattern of past hires.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the top of the ranking with past hires.

explain.text: The top of the ranking matches where past hires came from. That is bias from data: the pattern of the past, not a measure of who suits the role.

parts.question: What should the firm change first?

options.text: Use an approved tool with candidates' details removed, and check rankings across groups before they go out
Use a bigger and more capable chatbot for the ranking, and send the results as before
options.why: A bigger model learns the same pattern, and the data still leaves the firm.

options.text: Paste far more CVs into the chatbot next time, so its ranking has more data
options.why: More personal data in a public tool makes both problems worse.

options.text: Ask the chatbot to promise that its ranking of the candidates is fair
options.why: A promise from a chatbot is likely text, not a check.

feedback.correct: Fix both faults: the data that left the firm, and the unchecked bias.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The incident had two faults; fix both.

explain.text: The incident had two faults: personal data went into a public tool, and a biased ranking went out unchecked. An approved tool with details removed fixes the first; testing results across groups catches the second.

items.question: Put what to do before pasting anything into a chatbot in order.

lines.text: Check your employer's policy and which tools are approved
Remove names, numbers and details that identify anyone
Paste only the part the task needs
Check the output before you use it

feedback.correct: Policy, remove identifiers, paste only what is needed, check the output.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The policy decides whether to go on at all.

byKey.remove: Check the policy first: it may rule the tool out before anything is removed.
byKey.need: Remove identifiers before you choose what to paste.
byKey.output: Checking the output comes last, once there is output.

explain.text: The policy decides whether you may use the tool at all. Then remove what identifies anyone, paste only what the task needs, and check what comes back.

items.question: Write your rules as you would post them for the team.

widget.prompt: Write five rules for using chatbots at a small fund (invented), each with its reason in one or two sentences. Cover what may be pasted, checking outputs, bias, fakes, and one rule that reflects the measured-against-meant gap. Aim for 150 to 250 words.
widget.model:
1. **Paste nothing confidential into an outside tool.** No client data, passwords or unpublished research, unless our approved tool and policy allow it; what you paste leaves the firm and may be kept.
2. **Remove identifiers first.** Take out names, account numbers and details that combine to identify someone, because removing names alone is not enough.
3. **Check every specific figure, name and source before use.** A chatbot writes likely text, so estimate, recompute and read the cited page; "I am sure" is not a check.
4. **Test anything that decides about people across groups.** A model repeats the patterns in its examples, so compare its rates for each group before it screens a CV or a client.
5. **Call back before you pay.** Any payment request by voice, video or message is confirmed on the number in our own directory, because voices and writing can now be faked.

**Measured against meant.** When we reward a tool or a person for a number (ideas a week, chats closed), we ask what we really want and check that too, because a measure can be raised without the meaning.

rubric.text: A rule on what may not be pasted (client data, passwords, unpublished figures), with the policy and approved tools named as the exception
A rule on removing identifiers, noting that details can combine
A rule on checking figures, names and sources before use, with a reason tied to likely text
A rule on bias: test decisions across groups, because models copy their examples
A rule on fakes: confirm payment requests through a trusted channel
A rule or note on the gap between what is measured and what is meant

feedback.correct: Compare your rules with the model answer and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Good rules each name a risk from this level and give the reason in a sentence. The reason is what lets a colleague apply the rule to a case it does not mention.

items.question: A fund rewards a research assistant bot for the number of trade ideas it sends each week. What is the likely problem?

options.text: It sends many weak ideas, since the count rose and the quality was never measured
It sends only its best ideas, which is just what the fund wanted
options.why: The count rewards more ideas, not better ones.

options.text: None: more ideas is always better
options.why: More weak ideas waste the team's time. Quality was what was meant.

options.text: It stops sending ideas
options.why: Sending fewer would lower its reward.

feedback.correct: Count measured, quality meant: the bot raises the count.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the measure with what the fund wants.

explain.text: The fund meant useful ideas and measured how many. A bot can raise the count with weak ideas. That gap between measured and meant is the alignment problem in a small form.

items.question: A file of patients has no names. Tap the row that could still identify one person.

feedback.correct: A 101-year-old in a small village with a rare condition is very likely one person.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which combination fits only one person.

byKey.r0: Many 34-year-olds in a large city have asthma.
byKey.r2: Many 52-year-olds in a large city have back pain.

explain.text: No single detail is a name, but a very rare age, a small place and a rare condition together fit one person. Removing names is not enough when details combine.

items.question: A lender's test: the model approves 168 of 240 applicants in Group A and 99 of 180 in Group B, all with the same repayment records. How many percentage points apart are the approval rates?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each count into a rate first.

byKey.counts: You subtracted the counts. The groups differ in size, so compare rates.
byKey.ratio: You divided one rate by the other. The question asks how far apart they are.

explain.text: 168 of 240 is 70% and 99 of 180 is 55%, a gap of 15 points between applicants with the same records. The lender should find the cause before using the model.

items.question: Select all that apply: which are honest uses of AI tools?

options.text: Asking a chatbot to turn your own lecture notes into practice questions
Posting an AI-made picture with the label "AI image"
Having a chatbot tidy a complaint you wrote about a real problem
Posting chatbot reviews of your own product as "customers"
Handing in a chatbot's essay as your own where that is forbidden
options.why: That deceives the person marking it.

feedback.correct: The three uses that deceive no one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask in each case whether anyone is deceived.

explain.text: A tool is not a misuse in itself. Working on your own material, or labelling what the tool made, deceives no one. Posing as customers or hiding authorship does.

lines: We tried to deliver your parcel today.
Pay a £1.99 redelivery fee within 2 hours or it will be returned.
params.title: An invented message

items.question: A message arrives about a parcel. Tap every warning sign.

feedback.correct: The odd sender, the deadline with a fee, and the odd link.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for urgency, a payment request and addresses that do not match.

byKey.l2: A missed delivery is common in real messages too. On its own it is not a sign.
byKey.l5: A sign-off is no sign either way.

explain.text: An odd sender address, a deadline with a fee to pay, and a link to an odd site are the signs. The fluent wording proves nothing; check with the courier through its own website or app.
